<style>
/* Gwella base CSS · version 3.5.0 */
/* Base styles. Block CSS goes inside #page-container. The Base JS sets --thinqi-navbar-height and --anchor-section-offset; read them, never redeclare them. */

html {
  scroll-behavior: smooth;
}

.gwella {
  --primary-colour: #a3195b;
  --secondary-colour: #faf3f7;
}

.ytydysgu {
  --primary-colour: #325083;
  --secondary-colour: #f3f6fb;
}

body > main > article.plain-text {
  overflow: visible !important;
}

#page-container {
  --heading-1: 1.625rem;
  --heading-2: 1.375rem;
  --heading-3: 1.125rem;
  --numbered-subheading: 20px;

  /* Neutral colours, named for what they are used for (not for the colour), so a change says what it affects.
     They are the same in every theme; the theme colours are --primary-colour and --secondary-colour above. */
  --page-background: #fff;                                 /* behind the whole page */
  --text-on-primary: #fff;                                 /* text on a primary-coloured surface: buttons, the contents heading */
  --floating-button-background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.8);  /* the back-to-top button, over the content */
  --subheading-colour: #000;                               /* sub-headings (h3) in the content column */
  --card-text-colour: #000;                                /* text inside cards */
  --focus-ring-colour: #000;                               /* the outline that shows keyboard focus */
  --panel-background: #e8e8e8;                             /* the At a glance panel */
  --shadow-colour: #000;                                   /* shadows under cards and tiles (mixed with transparent for strength) */
  --divider-colour: #545454;                               /* the | between breadcrumb items */
  --secondary-text-colour: #545454;                        /* quieter text: the current page in the breadcrumb, the timestamp */
  --hover-background: #f1f1f1;                             /* background of a contents item under the pointer */
  --tile-border-colour: #d3d3d3;                           /* the border round an icon toggle tile */

  /* Deprecated: named for the colour, not the use. Kept as aliases so pages that use them keep working; removed in 3.6.0. */
  --dark-grey: var(--secondary-text-colour);
  --light-grey: var(--hover-background);
  --mid-grey: var(--tile-border-colour);

  --bs-font-sans-serif: "Noto Sans", "Noto Sans Arabic", sans-serif;
  --bs-body-font-family: "Noto Sans", "Noto Sans Arabic", sans-serif;

  margin-top: var(--thinqi-navbar-height, 95px);
  line-height: 160%;
  background-color: var(--page-background) !important;
  font-family: var(--bs-font-sans-serif) !important;

  &,
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }

  p {
    margin-block: 1em;
  }

  ul {
    list-style-type: disc;
    padding-left: 40px;
  }

  ol {
    list-style-type: decimal;
    padding-left: 40px;
    margin-block: 1em;
  }

  ol > li {
    display: list-item;
  }

  ol > li::marker {
    font-weight: bold;
  }

  li {
    line-height: 1.5em;
  }

  section {
    /* Padding, not margin, gives the 64px gap between sections. */
    padding-block: 1.25rem;
    scroll-margin-top: var(--anchor-section-offset, 145px);
  }

  h1,
  h2,
  h3,
  h4,
  h5 {
    font-weight: bold;
    margin-block: 1.5rem;
    /* Keeps anchored headings clear of the navbar. */
    scroll-margin-top: var(--anchor-section-offset, 145px);
  }

  a {
    color: var(--primary-colour);
    text-decoration: underline;

    &:hover {
      text-decoration: none;
    }
  }

  .standard-container {
    max-width: 860px;
    margin-inline: auto;

    @media (max-width: 1200px) {
      max-width: 750px;
    }

    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      max-width: 100%;
      padding-inline: 1.2rem;
    }
  }

  .content-column {
    h2 {
      font-size: var(--heading-2);
      font-weight: bold;
      margin-block: 1.5rem;
    }

    h3 {
      font-size: var(--heading-3);
      font-weight: 600;
      color: var(--subheading-colour);
    }

    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      display: contents;
    }
  }

  /* For an H2 directly below the page title (H1): pulls it up to close the gap.
     Same specificity as ".content-column h2" and later in the file, so it wins
     without !important. */
  h2.tight-heading {
    margin-top: -1rem;
  }

  .button-icon {
    margin-left: 0.25rem;
  }

  #breadcrumb-nav {
    padding: 1rem;

    #breadcrumb-nav__list {
      display: flex;
      align-items: center;
      flex-wrap: wrap;
      list-style: none;
      padding: 0;
      margin: 0;
      gap: 0.4rem;

      li:not(:last-child)::after {
        content: "|";
        margin-left: 0.5rem;
        color: var(--divider-colour);
      }

      li:last-child {
        color: var(--secondary-text-colour);
      }
    }

    a {
      color: var(--primary-colour);
      text-decoration: underline;

      &:hover {
        text-decoration: none;
      }
    }
  }

  .header {
    width: 100%;
  }

  #header-img {
    width: 100%;
    object-fit: cover;
    object-position: center 30%;
    display: block;

    @media (max-width: 576px) {
      object-fit: contain;
    }
  }

  #header-h1 {
    font-size: var(--heading-1);
    color: var(--primary-colour);
    line-height: 120%;
    font-weight: bold;
    margin-block: 1.5rem;

    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      order: 1;
    }
  }

  .main-grid {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 1.3fr 3fr;
    gap: 2rem;
    align-items: start;
    padding-inline: 1rem;

    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      grid-template-columns: 1fr;
      gap: 0;
    }
  }

  .content-body {
    margin-top: 1rem;

    /* The order belongs on .content-body, the grid item on mobile. */
    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      order: 4;
    }
  }

  #table-of-contents {
    position: sticky;
    top: 110px;

    @media (max-width: 768px) {
      order: 3;
      padding-top: 0;
      position: relative;
      top: 0;
    }

    #table-of-contents-heading {
      border-radius: 20px;
      background-color: var(--primary-colour);
      color: var(--text-on-primary);
      padding: 5px;
      text-align: center;
      font-weight: 400;
      line-height: 1.5;
      font-size: 1.2em;
      margin-block: 1.5rem 0.75em;
    }

    ul {
      padding-left: 0;
    }

    li {
      list-style: none;
      border-radius: 10px;
      padding: 10px;
      border: 1px solid var(--primary-colour);
      background-color: var(--secondary-colour);
      margin-left: 0;

      &:hover {
        background-color: var(--hover-background);
      }

      & + li {
        margin-top: 1rem;
      }
    }

    .toc-link {
      color: var(--primary-colour);

      &:hover {
        text-decoration: none;
      }
    }
  }

  .timestamp {
    margin-top: 2rem;
    margin-bottom: 1rem;
    font-style: italic;
    font-size: 13px;
    color: var(--secondary-text-colour);
    padding-inline: 1rem;
  }

  .back-to-top {
    display: none;
    flex-direction: column;
    position: fixed;
    right: 2rem;
    bottom: 2rem;
    background-color: var(--floating-button-background);
    border: none;
    justify-content: center;
    align-items: center;
    gap: 8px;
    color: var(--primary-colour);
    font-weight: bold;
    padding: 0.5rem 0.8rem;
    border-radius: 10px;
    cursor: pointer;
    z-index: 99;

    & > i {
      font-size: 30px;
      color: var(--primary-colour);
    }
  }

  /* ============================================================
     PLACE NEW BLOCK CSS ABOVE THIS LINE
     ============================================================ */
}
</style>

base.js:
<script>
// Gwella base JS · version 3.5.0
// The closing script tag near the end is escaped. Keep the backslash, or it ends this script early.
// Set the top margin and anchor offset for the page container.
// Also offsets for an optional #subnav, if the page has one.
function updateScrollOffset() {
  try {
    const thinqiNavbar =
      document.querySelector("div.app-chrome") ||
      document.querySelector(".public-site-header");
    const customSubnav = document.querySelector("#subnav");
    const isMobile = window.innerWidth <= 768;
    const thinqiNav_height = thinqiNavbar ? thinqiNavbar.offsetHeight : null;
    const customSubnav_height = customSubnav ? customSubnav.offsetHeight : null;
    let totalOffset = isMobile
      ? thinqiNav_height
      : thinqiNav_height + customSubnav_height;
    if (!thinqiNav_height && !customSubnav_height) {
      totalOffset = isMobile ? 137 : 145;
    }
    document.documentElement.style.setProperty(
      "--anchor-section-offset",
      totalOffset + "px",
    );
    const fallbackHeight = isMobile ? 137 : 95;
    if (thinqiNav_height > 0) {
      document.documentElement.style.setProperty(
        "--thinqi-navbar-height",
        thinqiNav_height + "px",
      );
    } else {
      document.documentElement.style.setProperty(
        "--thinqi-navbar-height",
        fallbackHeight + "px",
      );
    }
  } catch (error) {
    console.log("updateScrollOffset failed", error);
  }
}
window.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", updateScrollOffset);
window.addEventListener("resize", updateScrollOffset);
// Tooltips
const tooltipList = document.querySelectorAll('[data-bs-toggle="tooltip"]');
const tooltipTriggerList = [].slice.call(tooltipList);
tooltipTriggerList.forEach(
  (el) =>
    new bootstrap.Tooltip(el, {
      container: el,
    }),
);
// Back to top
const backToTopBtn = document.querySelector(".back-to-top");
if (backToTopBtn) {
  window.addEventListener("scroll", () => {
    const isTabletOrMobileView = window.innerWidth <= 768;
    const threshold = isTabletOrMobileView
      ? window.innerHeight
      : window.innerHeight / 2;
    backToTopBtn.style.display = window.scrollY < threshold ? "none" : "flex";
  });
  backToTopBtn.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    e.stopPropagation();
    window.scrollTo({ top: 0, behavior: "smooth" });
  });
}
</script>

section.label: Section
section.description: Start here for every new bit of content — wraps it in a properly-idd <section> with its heading, and generates the matching table-of-contents entry at the same time, so those two ids can never drift apart.
section.htmlOutputLabel: HTML for this section — paste into .content-body, then paste other blocks' content where marked
section.secondaryLabel: Table of contents entry — paste inside <nav id="table-of-contents">

fields.label: This section comes directly below the page title
fields.help: Tick this for the first section on a page that has no At a glance box. It closes the large gap between the page title and this heading.

section.guide:
Think of this as starting a new chapter in a book — before you write anything, you give the chapter a title, add it to the contents page at the front, and set up a blank page for it to live on. That's exactly what this does, in one go.

The HTML — two pieces, two destinations

This is the one block that produces two separate outputs, because a table of contents entry and the actual section live in two different places on the page. The section wrapper:

<section id="putting-into-practice"> <h2>Putting into practice</h2> (content goes here) </section>

...and, separately, the matching table of contents entry:

<li><a href="#putting-into-practice" class="toc-link">Putting into practice</a></li>

Notice the id (putting-into-practice) and the link's href are exactly the same text — that's what makes clicking the table of contents entry actually jump down to this section. Both get built from the same title you type, once, so there's no way for them to quietly drift apart the way hand-typed ids sometimes do.

The "directly below the page title" tick box

Headings normally keep a generous gap above them. That's right between sections, but when the very first section sits straight under the page title (a page with no At a glance box) the gap looks too big. Ticking the box adds class="tight-heading" to the heading, and the Base CSS pulls it up. Leave it unticked for every other section, and for pages that do have an At a glance box.

Where the other blocks fit in

The comment in the middle — <!-- Content goes here --> — is where you paste whatever you build on the other tabs: an image-text-section, an accordion, at-a-glance, anything. One section can hold more than one block if the content calls for it; just paste them one after another in place of the comment.

Why there's no CSS output for this one

Unlike every other tab, this block doesn't need its own CSS — spacing, scroll behaviour and heading styles for sections are already part of the Base CSS every page starts with, so there's nothing extra to add.

nav-cards.label: Navigation cards
nav-cards.description: A row of cards, two styles available: icon + description + button (only the button is clickable, unlike resource-cards), or numbered heading + plain icon with no button at all. Choose the style once — it applies to every card in the row.
nav-cards.guide:
Two styles live in this one block, chosen once for the whole row via "Card style":

Style 1 — Icon + description + button

Three (or however many) signposts side by side — an icon, a line explaining what's over there, and a button to actually go. The important bit: only the button is clickable, not the whole card — unlike resource-cards, where the entire card is one big link.

<div class="nav-card"> <div class="nav-card__icon"> <img src="..." alt="" /> </div> <p>Learn what compassionate leadership means</p> <a href="..." class="nav-card__button">Understand it</a> </div>

Notice the <img> and the <a> button are separate elements, not nested inside one another — that's the structural difference from resource-cards, where the whole card is one clickable link. Here, clicking the icon or the description text does nothing; only the button is an actual link.

The circle behind the icon (style 1 only)

The coloured circle isn't part of the icon image at all — it's plain CSS, a box made perfectly round with border-radius: 50%, filled with the page's main colour, with the icon centred inside it using flexbox. That's why the icon itself needs to be a transparent PNG: the coloured circle is the actual background, showing through wherever the icon image is transparent. A white-icon-on-transparent-background PNG is what makes this look right — a PNG with its own solid background would show up as an ugly box over the circle instead of blending in.

New tab, off by default (style 1 only)

Unlike buttons and resource-cards (which default to opening in a new tab), this block defaults to the same tab — matching the reference design, where these are meant to feel like in-site navigation rather than links out to something external. Ticking the box adds target="_blank" and the little arrow icon, same as everywhere else.

Style 2 — Numbered heading + plain icon

No visible button — but the whole card is clickable, using the same trick as resource-cards.

<div class="nav-card nav-card--numbered"> <a href="..." class="stretched-link" aria-label="..."></a> <h3><span class="nav-card__number">1.</span> Agree direction and ensure alignment and commitment</h3> <div class="nav-card__icon-plain"> <img src="..." alt="" /> </div> </div>

That empty <a class="stretched-link"> has no visible content of its own — stretched-link is what invisibly expands its clickable area to cover the entire card, the same way resource-cards works. The aria-label is filled in automatically from the heading text, so a screen reader still announces something meaningful even though there's no visible link text to read. Hovering the card lifts it slightly and adds a shadow (matching the lift effect used on resource cards and icon-toggle triggers), and the cursor switches to a pointer — both there specifically to signal "this whole box is clickable" even though nothing looks like a traditional button.

Two more things worth knowing: the icon here has no coloured circle behind it — these icons are already full-colour transparent PNGs with their own colours baked in, so no CSS circle is needed or wanted. And numbering is automatic (a checkbox, on by default) rather than typed — the number is based on each card's position, so reordering or removing a card never leaves you with "1, 3, 4" or a stale number stuck on the wrong card.

How the icon always sits at the bottom

margin-top: auto on the icon's wrapper is a neat flexbox trick — inside a flex column, an automatic margin greedily eats up all the leftover space above it, pushing everything after it to the very bottom of the box. That's what keeps the icons lined up at the bottom of every card even when headings run to different lengths.

at-a-glance.label: At-a-glance
at-a-glance.description: A short bulleted summary box that sits above the table of contents on the page.
at-a-glance.guide:
Think of this like the little summary box you sometimes see at the top of a recipe, before the actual steps — a quick "here's what you're getting" before the reader dives into the page.

The HTML

It's just a box with a heading and a list:

<div id="at-a-glance"> <h3 id="at-a-glance-heading">At a glance</h3> <ul> <li>Your bullet point</li> </ul> </div>

The heading text "At a glance" never changes, so the tool writes it for you — one less thing to type or accidentally misspell. Each <li> is one bullet; add or remove as many as you like in the form and the tool builds the list to match.

The CSS

id="at-a-glance" is how the CSS finds this exact box to give it its grey background and the coloured line underneath (the page's main colour). border-radius: 20px 20px 0 0 means "round the top-left and top-right corners, leave the bottom two square" — that's why it looks like a rounded card sitting on a flat base.

li + li { margin-top: 10px; } means "add a gap above any bullet that comes right after another bullet" — the + is CSS-speak for "the one right after". That's why the first bullet sits flush at the top, but every bullet after it gets a bit of breathing room.

On mobile

order: 2 is like a seating chart that only applies on small screens — it tells this box "you're in seat 2" so it lands in the right spot (title, then this box, then the table of contents, then everything else) even though the actual HTML order underneath never changes.

hero-text.label: Hero text
hero-text.description: Sits just below at-a-glance and just above the first section — one rich text editor, same as elsewhere. The first paragraph you write is automatically rendered larger (1.25em); everything after it is normal size. No separate field for the opening line — the tool finds it for you.

fields.label: Content
fields.placeholder: Write freely — the first paragraph is automatically styled larger...

hero-text.guide:
The bit of writing that greets the reader right after the summary box — one editor, write it exactly like any other rich text field. The only special thing about this block is what happens automatically to whatever paragraph comes first.

Write normally — the sizing takes care of itself

You don't tell the tool which paragraph is the "opening" one, and there's no separate box for it. As you type, the tool looks at your finished content and finds the very first paragraph, wherever it is, and marks it:

<p class="hero-text__intro">Your opening sentence.</p> <p>Everything else, at normal size.</p>

The size (1.25em, a quarter bigger than normal text) lives on that hero-text__intro class in the CSS, not on the text itself — so it's always applied to whatever the first paragraph turns out to be, structurally guaranteed, rather than depending on someone remembering to size it themselves every time they write one of these.

Everything else

This is the exact same rich text editor used elsewhere in the tool (headings, bold, italic, lists, links) — full flexibility. The only thing that's different about the output is that one added class on the first paragraph.

image-text-section.label: Image-text-section
image-text-section.description: Text that wraps around a small image or video and flows underneath it once it passes the media's height. Use it when the writing is the main thing and the media is a supporting extra. The media is optional. If you want a clean side-by-side split instead, use Equal columns or Media beside text.

fields.label: Content
fields.placeholder: Write the content that sits alongside the image or video...

image-text-section.guide:
In 30 seconds

Text that wraps around a picture or video, like a photo in a newspaper column. The media is told to float to one side, and the text flows around it, then underneath once it passes the bottom of the picture.

The media is optional: with none, you just get your text.

See it on your own block. Open the Explain tab beside the preview, turn on X-ray, and hover the image: the code line for the picture lights up and tells you about float.

The idea: float

Picture a newspaper column with a photo tucked into the corner and the text flowing around it, wrapping underneath once it runs past the photo's height. That is exactly what this block does.

<div class="image-text-section"> <img src="..." alt="..." /> <div> (your content goes here) </div> </div>

Two things sit inside the wrapper: the media, then a div holding whatever you wrote. Whatever you used (headings, bullet points, plain paragraphs) is carried through as real HTML.

Why the order matters

The media comes first in the code. A floated picture can only sit beside text that comes after it, so putting it first is what lets the text wrap round it. Move it below the text and it would drop underneath instead.

The "Large" size

Choosing "Large" adds a class, media-large, which makes the picture bigger (340px rather than 275px). That is how the old "badge" style, such as the pledge certificate graphic, was folded into this block.

On phones

There is not room to put things side by side on a small screen. The CSS switches the float off and shows the picture full width above the text instead.

Deep dive: floats and the "clearfix"

float: right is an old but very useful CSS trick. It pulls the image out to the right-hand side and lets the text in the neighbouring div flow around it like water round a rock.

The catch: a floated element no longer counts towards its parent's height, so it can spill out of its own box and overlap whatever comes next. This rule stops that:

.image-text-section::after { content: ""; display: block; clear: both; }

It adds an invisible block at the end of the wrapper that refuses to sit beside any float. That forces the wrapper to grow tall enough to contain the picture. It is called a "clearfix", and you will see it in plenty of CSS.

accordion.label: Accordion
accordion.description: A stack of expandable items — only one open at a time. This block only builds the structure (titles + correctly-linked ids); the content inside each panel is left as a placeholder for you to fill in — paste generated content from another tab, or write it directly.

fields.label: Group name (used to build a readable id — leave blank to fall back to a random id)

accordion.guide:
In 30 seconds

An accordion is a list of titles that each hide a panel. Click a title and its panel slides open; open another and the first one closes.

It all hinges on one trick: every title and its panel share a name. The builder writes both names for you, from the same words, so they can never drift apart.

See it on your own accordion. Open the Explain tab beside the preview, then hover data-bs-target in the code and watch the matching names light up.

The idea: a button that knows its panel by name

Think of a filing cabinet: each drawer has a label, you click the label to slide the drawer open, and, because this is a well-behaved cabinet, opening one drawer closes whichever one was already open.

The button doesn't know what "Digital literacy" means. It only knows a name to look for, like dialling a phone number:

<button data-bs-target="#collapse-digital-literacy" ...>Digital literacy</button> <div id="collapse-digital-literacy" ...>(your content goes here)</div>

The # means "the element with this id". Bootstrap's script (already loaded by the base HTML) finds the panel with that id and opens it.

What goes wrong when the names don't match

If the two names differ by even one letter, clicking the title does nothing at all, and there is no error message to tell you why. This is the most common way a hand-edited accordion breaks. It is why the builder writes both names from the same title: there is nothing to mistype.

"Only one open at a time"

Every panel also carries data-bs-parent="#accordion-…", naming the accordion it belongs to. Bootstrap reads that as an instruction: "when I open, ask every other panel in this group to close." No custom code is needed.

The "Group name" field

It only gives the whole accordion a readable name (for example accordion-digital-literacy-resources instead of a random one). It is for the humans who read the pasted code later and changes nothing about how it behaves.

Deep dive: what happens when you click a title
  1. You click the button. Because it has data-bs-toggle="collapse", Bootstrap's script takes over.
  2. It reads data-bs-target and looks up the element with that id.
  3. It adds the class show to the panel (the collapse class hides it otherwise) and removes collapsed from the button, which is what turns the arrow.
  4. It flips aria-expanded to "true", so screen readers announce that the panel is open.
  5. It reads data-bs-parent, finds the other panels in that group, and closes them the same way.

Our CSS only changes how this looks (the arrow, the underline, no borders). The behaviour is entirely Bootstrap's.

icon-toggle.label: Icon-toggle
icon-toggle.description: A grid of clickable icons; clicking one reveals its own content panel below (and closes any other open panel). Content is left as a placeholder for you to fill in, same as accordion. Note: only one icon-toggle group per page — the click behaviour tracks 'the currently open panel' globally, not per-group.

fields.label: Group name (used to build a readable id — leave blank to fall back to a random id)

icon-toggle.guide:
Imagine a row of light switches: flick one, and a message board underneath lights up with that switch's message. Flick a different one, and the board swaps to the new message — only one message shows at a time.

The HTML

<div onclick="openAccordion(this, 'content-hosting-a-meeting')" ...> <div class="data-icon-card"> <img src="..." /> <h5>Hosting a meeting</h5> </div> </div> <div class="content-display" id="content-hosting-a-meeting"> (content goes here) </div>

Clicking an icon calls a function called openAccordion, telling it two things: "here's the icon I clicked" and "here's the id of the panel it should open" — like calling a friend and saying "open that box, and close whatever else is open." That id has to match the panel's own id exactly, which is why the tool generates both from the same label text automatically.

Why the JS is separate from the HTML/CSS

Unlike the accordion (which reuses Bootstrap's own built-in behaviour), this block needs its own small helper function — openAccordion — that isn't part of Bootstrap. It only needs to exist once on the page no matter how many icons you add, which is why it's pasted into the shared script area rather than repeated per icon — like one shared tool in a toolbox, not a new copy for every job.

The scroll behaviour

When a panel opens, the page automatically scrolls down to it (scrollIntoView) — with some extra breathing room added above it, deliberately, so the icon you just clicked stays visible on screen. That way you can find it again to close the panel without having to scroll back up.

resource-cards.label: Resource cards
resource-cards.description: A grid of linked resource cards — image, title, type, and an optional duration/length. Generates just the card grid; wrap it in your own <section> with a heading, same as every other block.
resource-cards.guide:
Picture a stack of business cards laid out in a neat grid — each one clickable, each one the same height as its neighbours in the same row, however short or long its title happens to be.

The HTML

<div class="card"> <img src="..." class="resource-card__img" /> <div> <a href="..." class="stretched-link" target="_blank"> <strong>Title text <i class="fa-solid fa-up-right-from-square"></i></strong> </a> <p><strong>Type</strong><span>Duration</span></p> </div> </div>

The stretched-link class is a neat CSS trick: it stretches the clickable area of that link invisibly to cover the entire card, even though the actual link text is only a few words. That's why clicking anywhere on the card — the image, the empty space, not just the title — opens the link.

Why every card in a row matches height

By default, a grid lets each item size itself to fit its own content — so a card with a two-line title would end up shorter than one with a three-line title next to it. Telling the grid to stretch instead makes every card fill the full height of its row, and then the card's own layout (a flexbox column with justify-content: space-between) pushes the type/duration line down to the bottom either way — like a bookend holding the price tag at the bottom of the shelf no matter how thick the book is.

The new-tab checkbox

Ticking it adds target="_blank" and the little arrow icon, tied to the one checkbox so neither can be forgotten. The builder also adds rel="noopener noreferrer" (a safety measure for links that open a new tab) but only to external links. Relative links and links to our own domains (listed in INTERNAL_HOSTS) keep just target="_blank".

buttons.label: Buttons
buttons.description: A row of call-to-action buttons (e.g. 'Sign the pledge'). Wraps as needed on smaller screens.
buttons.guide:
The simplest block here — a row of "go do this" buttons, like "Sign the pledge" or "Download the guide".

The HTML

<div class="buttons"> <a href="..." target="_blank" aria-label="Sign the pledge (opens in a new tab)"> Sign the pledge <i class="fa-solid fa-up-right-from-square"></i> </a> </div>

The aria-label is what a screen reader announces instead of the visible text — it's there so someone who can't see the little arrow icon still gets told "this link opens in a new tab" out loud. Both the icon and that spoken warning are tied to the same "open in a new tab" checkbox, so they always agree with each other; you'll never end up with the icon showing but the label not mentioning it, or vice versa.

The CSS

display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; on the row means the buttons sit side by side and automatically drop onto a new line if they run out of horizontal space — no extra work needed for that to happen responsively.

flex-section.label: Flex-section
flex-section.description: Text on the left, media on the right, in two equal-width columns that are vertically centred, for a balanced, symmetrical look. The text is always on the left (it can't be flipped) and the media is required. To put the media on the left, or to line it up with the top of the text, use Media beside text instead.

fields.label: Left column — content
fields.placeholder: Write the content for this side...

flex-section.guide:
Picture a book lying open — content on the left-hand page, a picture or video on the right-hand page, side by side, both taking up roughly equal space. That's the whole idea of this block, and it's genuinely different from image-text-section: nothing wraps around anything here, it's a clean two-column split.

The HTML

<div class="flex-section"> <div class="text-content"> (your content goes here) </div> <div class="video-content"> <iframe src="..."></iframe> </div> </div>

The CSS

display: flex on the outer wrapper lines the two inner boxes up side by side. flex: 1 on both of them means "split the available space evenly between us" — like cutting a sandwich exactly in half, regardless of how wide the page actually is.

On phones, flex-direction: column switches that same layout from side-by-side to stacked — the same two boxes, just rearranged vertically once the screen gets too narrow for two columns to sit comfortably next to each other.

Why media is required here

Unlike image-text-section, there's no "None" option for the right column — an empty second column wouldn't make sense in a layout whose entire point is two columns side by side.

The "Another content block" option

Picking this for the right column doesn't generate any media at all — it just leaves a marker instead:

<div class="video-content"> <!-- CONTENT BLOCK GOES HERE --> </div>

Same idea as the placeholder used in accordion and icon-toggle panels: build whatever you actually need on another tab (buttons, for instance) and paste its generated HTML in place of that comment. This block only ever handles the two-column structure itself — it doesn't try to generate every possible thing that could go in the right column.

two-column.description: Media in one column and text in the other, both lined up at the top, with the text column a little wider. You choose which side the media sits on. Best for longer text with a smaller picture beside it. For a balanced, centred, equal split use Equal columns instead.

two-column.guide:
Think of a magazine spread: a photo on one page, the story on the other. This block is that layout, with the photo on the left by default.

Flip the layout

The Layout option switches the media to the right. The HTML stays in the same order either way; the change is made in CSS, so the text is always read after the media by screen readers.

Mobile

On phones the two columns stack, media first, and the image is shown at 3:2 and centred.

Buttons in the text column

Build buttons on the Buttons tab, then paste their HTML into the text column. Inside a two-column layout they automatically become full width and stack with a gap.
